title: Higher-Order Functions Check
description: Predict the output length and content of map/filter pipelines.

options.text: A function that takes a function as an argument, returns a function, or both
Any function declared with `function` instead of an arrow
A function that always returns a number
A function that cannot be reassigned

questions.explanation: Higher-order functions operate on other functions — by accepting them as arguments and/or returning them.
`map` returns a new array with each element transformed by the callback, keeping the same length as the input.

questions.prompt:
```js
console.log(["a", "", "b", ""].filter((s) => s !== ""));
```
What is the length of the printed array?
questions.explanation: `filter` keeps only elements where the predicate is truthy. Only `"a"` and `"b"` pass, so the result has length 2.

questions.prompt: After `const result = [1, 2, 3].map((n) => n * 2);`, what is the original array?
questions.explanation: `map` never mutates the array it is called on — it always returns a brand-new array.

questions.prompt: Can the result of `filter` be shorter than the input array?

options.text: No, `filter` always returns the same length as the input
Yes, only elements where the predicate returns truthy are kept
No, `filter` throws if any element is removed
Only if the input array is empty

questions.explanation: Unlike `map`, `filter` can shrink the array — every element that fails the predicate is dropped from the result.
`pipeline` composes the steps in order: trim first ("hi"), then uppercase ("HI"). `pipeline` itself is higher-order — it takes functions and returns one.
